context.title: Where the TMEM read fits in attention
context.summary: This GQA kernel forms query–key scores, converts them into softmax weights, and accumulates weighted values in tensor memory (TMEM). Warp 2 allocates and frees the score and output accumulators; warps 4–7 read them. The final output-accumulator read is the useful source focus for the release question. The retained model instruction IDs have no supplied PTX or issuer binding, so this walkthrough does not identify them with that site. With the saved sequence length and scalar inputs, every CTA has two 128-key tiles to process; the zero-work exits are not taken.

context.evidence_title: Check the workload, roles and accumulator journey

steps.label: Why two tiles really execute
steps.text: The batch index is `ctaid.x / 8 = 0`, so thread 0 stages `seq_len[0] = 2048` at shared offset `108148`; its copy wait and the cluster barrier precede the shared read. Parameter 12 is zero. Substitution in the partition arithmetic gives `r205 = 2048`, `r210 = 16`, `r213 = 2`, `r217 = 0`, and therefore work count `r11 = 2` and start tile `r14 = 2 × ctaid.z`. The eight z positions cover keys `256z…256z+255`. In the reader loop the counter starts at −2 and reaches zero after two iterations. Thus the exits at 5496–5501, 6583 and 6801 do not bypass this work.

steps.label: Which threads own the protocol
steps.text: The thread selector comes from `%tid.x`, shifted right by five and broadcast within a warp. The dispatch selects warp 2 for allocation/MMA/release, warp 1 for K/V loads, warp 0 for Q loads, and warps 4–7 for the reader path; warp 3 branches to the final CTA barrier. With a 256-thread block, the release handshake therefore includes 32 allocator threads and 128 readers. Allocation and arrival are outside the elected-lane blocks used for individual MMA/commit instructions.

steps.label: How the two accumulators are used
steps.text: Q and K TMA destinations feed the first MMA accumulator, whose handle is stored at shared offset `108128`; the output accumulator handle is at `108144`. Each allocation requests 32 TMEM columns, not 32 bytes. Score MMA starts with accumulation disabled for each tile. Readers explicitly wait for the score load, scale the values, compute maxima and exponentials, and stage BF16 weights in shared memory. The first weighted-value MMA initializes the output accumulator; the final tile accumulates into it. Between tiles, readers load, rescale and write the previous output partial. The final read stages cluster-shared partials; the subsequent shared reductions and division produce the global BF16 output `o`.

sections.title: Final read: half the lanes bypass result use
sections.answer: After the final output MMA is ready, all four reader warps issue the TMEM load. Lanes 0–15 in each warp use its eight result registers in cluster-shared stores; lanes 16–31 skip those stores. Both paths reach the same release arrival, with no intervening load-completion wait. This establishes a load-issue-to-arrival path, but the skipped stores cannot establish completion of the bypassing lanes’ reads. Another lane receiving its result registers does not establish completion of the bypassing lanes’ reads. The relevant question is whether those reads complete before their release arrivals.

code.caption: Final read, conditional transfer, common release arrival

sections.evidence_title: Check the branch and compare every TMEM read site

steps.label: Why the split is exactly half of each reader warp
steps.text: The mask is applied to `%r5 = %tid.x`, not a model actor ID. Within reader threads 128–255, `tid.x & 16` is zero for lanes 0–15 and nonzero for lanes 16–31. The `setp.ne` and taken branch skip all eight stores at 7380–7401 and land immediately before the common barrier-address setup and arrival. The diagram displays the first store as the representative transfer. Neither edge skips the final load or the arrival.

steps.label: What the other load sites establish
steps.text: The score read has an explicit `tcgen05.wait::ld` on every iteration. The later-tile rescale read instead uses all eight loaded values in arithmetic, writes them back to TMEM, and performs `tcgen05.wait::st`; that wait tracks stores, not loads. It is therefore inaccurate to call the final read the only load without an adjacent load wait. At the final read, the lane-dependent bypass additionally removes the local result use for half the lanes. The PTX 9.2 `tcgen05.ld` specification describes an asynchronous operation: `.sync.aligned` coordinates warp issuance and is not itself a completion wait.

rows: Use all results → store → store wait

code.caption: Explicit load wait versus result-dependent rescaling

steps.label: Why the preceding MMA wait does not finish this load
steps.text: The output-ready barrier at shared offset `108064` starts with count 1. Warp 2 commits the first and final output MMA groups to it. The readers skip its first loop wait while `r1104 = 0`; on the second tile they wait with parity 0 and toggle `%r1122` to 1. The final wait at 7365 therefore tests parity 1 before issuing the final load. This orders the producer’s MMA completion before reading its result; it cannot finish the new load issued afterward. PTX uses `tcgen05.commit` for MMA/copy/shift completion and `tcgen05.wait::ld` for load completion.

sections.title: Release handshake: the second phase waits for all readers
sections.answer: The release barrier does include all 128 readers, including the lanes that skip stores. Together with 32 allocator-thread arrivals they complete its second phase; warp 2 polls parity 1 and frees both TMEM allocations only after that poll succeeds. The missing guarantee lies before notification: every reader’s asynchronous TMEM read must be complete before its release arrival can stand for “finished reading.” The arrival count proves participation, not that completion condition. This source relation explains the lifecycle question without asserting an observed premature free.

The dashed edge is the completion condition needed to turn the reader notification into a safe-release guarantee; it is not a hardware schedule or a mapping of the retained instruction IDs. The store path still has to arrive: bypassing lanes alone cannot release the allocator.

sections.evidence_title: Check both phases and the completion boundary

steps.label: The barrier is reused, with different literal parities
steps.text: One elected lane of warp 0 initializes shared offset `108080` with expected count 160. PTX initialization starts phase 0 with zero pending transaction bytes. The first round publishes the allocated handles: all 32 allocator threads arrive after allocation, and all 128 readers arrive before waiting with parity 0. The release round uses the same address, with allocator and reader arrivals after their work; the allocator tests parity 1. No transaction expectation or `tcgen05.commit` attaches load completion to this barrier.

steps.label: Why these really are separate phases
steps.text: A thread’s second arrival cannot be assigned phase 1 merely from its position in the listing. Here an intervening dependency establishes the transition. Before computing, warp 2 waits on the input-ready barrier at shared offset `107920`, initialized with count 6. Its first round needs one elected Q-loader arrival, one elected K-loader arrival, and four elected reader-warp arrivals. Those reader arrivals occur only after the readers’ successful parity-0 wait on `108080`. The input-ready wait therefore prevents the allocator from reaching its later release arrival before the first handshake has completed. Q and K also contribute expected TMA bytes (1,024 and 16,384); those transactions do not attach the later TMEM reads to the release barrier.

steps.label: The later shared-memory waits serve another object
steps.text: After the release arrival, readers wait on cluster partial-result barriers at offsets `108096` and `108112`. Their `st.async` transactions stage statistics and output partials in shared memory; the epilogue consumes those partials and writes global `o`. These waits occur after notification to the allocator and are not a replacement for completing the TMEM read before that notification. The final CTA barrier likewise occurs after the allocator’s deallocations. The saved witness lacks source/issuer bindings, so the precise correspondence between these static sites and the retained failed orders remains open.

sections.title: Numerical model: the score reduction is a separate limitation
sections.answer: The saved value-model diagnostic names the warp maximum reduction used while forming softmax weights. The supplied PTX shows the first reduction consuming a scaled score; it is not a TMEM deallocation operation. Its missing exact per-thread value model and the unmet lifecycle prerequisite are distinct obstacles to a numerical conclusion. Neither is evidence that this arithmetic produced an incorrect answer.

sections.evidence_title: Check the reduction input and saved analysis limits

steps.label: The configured score reaches the reduction
steps.text: The score index is `tid.x − 128 + 256z` on the first tile and 128 greater on the second. Both are within `[0, 2048)` for the supplied grid, and parameter 12 makes the lower limit zero. The in-range branch at 6949 bypasses the negative-infinity replacement. The scale comes from parameter 11, loaded into `%r129`; multiplication produces `%r822`, then `redux.sync.max.NaN.f32` produces `%r81`. This traces the operation named by the value-model diagnostic without claiming a completed numerical comparison.

next.text: Resolve the event-to-source and issuer binding for the retained TMEM load and frees, then check how the verifier and the PTX completion contract represent each reader’s load completion before the release arrival. The final read’s bypass lanes are the specific source path to examine; the rescale read should be distinguished using its register dependencies and store wait. Numerical work also needs an exact value model for the reported `redux` operation after its prerequisites are satisfied.
